OpenFOAM v2606, simpleFoam: steady, incompressible Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes with Menter's k-omega SST turbulence model, second-order upwind for momentum, wall functions at every surface.
Forces are the mean of the last 400 iterations; the figure after each is twice the standard deviation over them, which is how much the answer still wanders.

snappyHexMesh wrapped round each vehicle's own surfaces, exported straight from its build: 4.4 million cells for the car, fans off, 4.6 million fans on, and 3.5 million for the Nyx. Half of each vehicle, with a symmetry plane down its centreline.
Cells of 6 mm on the car's surfaces, 3 to 12 mm on the Nyx's, finer on the flying surfaces' leading edges.

The car at 50 m/s over a road moving at the same speed, its wheels turning at road speed, the ground plane 8 mm up so each tyre has a contact patch. Each fan as two faces across its shroud, drawing 4 m³/s out ahead of the rotor and returning it behind.
The Nyx at 100 m/s (Mach 0.29) in free air, gear up and doors shut, its intakes and nozzles capped as a powered-off wind-tunnel model is, moments about its combat centre of gravity.

RANS with wall functions and no boundary-layer cells is a good judge of pressure forces, which is where downforce, lift and most of the drag come from, and a poor judge of skin friction and separation from smooth surfaces. There is one mesh per case, not a mesh-independence study, so treat differences under about 10 % as within the method's reach.
The fans-off car had its intakes shut, which a stopped fan comes close to; the Nyx runs have no engine flow, so its drag is without the inlets' spillage or the jets' effect on the afterbody.
The export, case generator and post-processing are in the model gallery's aero/study folder. With OpenFOAM installed:

blender -b car.blend -P tools/export_stl.py -- cases/vx1/geometry.json runs/vx1/constant/triSurface
python3 tools/make_case.py cases/vx1/case.json runs/vx1
openfoam -c runs/vx1/Allrun
